claims.claim: Virtual screening of ~2.5 million small organic molecules in the Enamine in-stock library was performed against the binding site of repaglinide (RPG) in the RPG-bound KATP channel cryoEM structure (PDB ID 6PZ9).
claims.source: Using an Artificial Intelligence (AI) virtual screening system AtomNet developed by Atomwise (Atomwise AIMS Program, 2024; Gniewek et al., 2021; Wallach et al., 2015), we performed virtual screening of ~2.5 million small organic molecules in the Enamine in-stock library against the binding site of a high affinity KATP inhibitor pharmacochaperone, RPG, resolved in our published RPG-bound KATP channel (hamster SUR1 plus rat Kir6.2) cryoEM structure (PDB ID 6PZ9; ~3.65 Å) (Atomwise AIMS Program, 2024; Martin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the virtual screening methodology.

claims.claim: The RPG binding site being screened involves the following residues: R306, Y377, A380, I381, W430, F433, L434, N437, M441, T588, L592, L593, S595, V596, T1242, N1245, R1246, E1249, W1297, R1300 of the SUR1 subunit and residues M1, L2, S3, K5, G6, I7 of Kir6.2.
claims.source: The RPG binding site being screened involves the following residues: R306, Y377, A380, I381, W430, F433, L434, N437, M441, T588, L592, L593, S595, V596, T1242, N1245, R1246, E1249, W1297, R1300 of the SUR1 subunit (chain C in PDB ID 6PZ9) and residues M1, L2, S3, K5, G6, I7 of Kir6.2 (chain D in PDB ID 6PZ9) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The top 96 predicted binders were subjected to biochemical and functional testing.
claims.source: Following diversity clustering to minimize selection of structurally similar scaffolds and filtering for oral availability as well as excluding toxicophores (see Methods for details), the top 96 predicted binders (Supplementary file 1) were subjected to subsequent biochemical and functional testing as described below.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental workflow.

claims.claim: Three compounds (C24, C27, and C45) showed consistent pharmacochaperone effects in two independent screening experiments.
claims.source: Treatment with some of the test compounds yielded weak or moderate upper SUR1F27S band, suggesting pharmacochaperone effects. We selected three compounds that showed consistent results in two independent screening experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) for further testing in a different assay.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: C24, C27, and C45 correspond to ZINC IDs Z1607618869, Z2068224500, and Z1620764636, respectively.
claims.source: The three compounds selected, C24, C27, and C45, correspond to ZINC database (https://zinc.docking.org/) ID: Z1607618869, Z2068224500, and Z1620764636, respectively, and represent diverse chemical scaffolds, as shown in Figure 1B.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: All three compounds (C24, C27, and C45) inhibited KATP channel currents.
claims.source: Inside-out patch-clamp recordings of cells expressing KATP channels (hamster WT SUR1+rat WT Kir6.2) showed that indeed, all three compounds inhibited KATP channel currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Compound Z1620764636 (C45) showed a clear dose-dependent inhibition, with an estimated steady-state IC50 between 1 and 10 μM, and clear current recovery upon compound washout.
claims.source: Of the three compounds Z1620764636 (C45) showed a clear dose-dependent inhibition, with an estimated steady-state IC50 between 1 and 10 μM, and clear current recovery upon compound washout (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Ci).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Ci.

claims.claim: Overnight treatment with 100 μM Aekatperone led to a clear increase of the mature upper band for SUR1A30T, SUR1A116P, and SUR1V187D trafficking mutants.
claims.source: Overnight treatment with 100 μM Aekatperone led to a clear increase of the mature upper band (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The pharmacochaperone effect of Aekatperone on SUR1A30T was already evident at 10 μM and became more pronounced as the concentration increased, with the effect plateauing between 100 and 200 μM.
claims.source: A detailed dose-response for SUR1A30T showed that the pharmacochaperone effect of Aekatperone was already evident at 10 μM and became more pronounced as the concentration increased, with the effect plateauing between 100 and 200 μM (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: At 200 μM Aekatperone, the intensity of the upper band relative to the total intensity of both lower and upper bands for SUR1A30T was 64.21 ± 3.35% of that observed for WT SUR1.
claims.source: At 200 μM, the intensity of the upper band relative to the total intensity of both lower and upper bands for SUR1A30T was 64.21 ± 3.35% of that observed for WT SUR1 (n=3, p=0.0133 by Student's t-test) based on densitometry by ImageJ (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Upon Aekatperone treatment, there was a clear increase in the percentage of cells showing surface staining of SUR1F27S or SUR1A30T mutant channels.
claims.source: Upon Aekatperone treatment, there was a clear increase in the percentage of cells showing surface staining of SUR1F27S or SUR1A30T mutant channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top panels), providing direct evidence that Aekatperone rescues surface expression of CHI-causing SUR1 trafficking mutations.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP on KATP channels.
claims.source: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP, but MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone.
claims.source: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP, but MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2.
claims.source: Importantly, the pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
claims.source: Importantly, the pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of protein sequences.

claims.claim: Aekatperone dose-dependently reduced Rb+ efflux in WT KATP channels, with an IC50 of 9.23 µM±0.36 µM.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3A, Aekatperone dose-dependently reduced Rb+ efflux, with an IC50 of 9.23 µM±0.36 µM (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: For both SUR1F27S and SUR1A30T mutants, a significant increase in Rb+ efflux was observed in cells treated with Aekatperone in a dose-dependent manner compared with cells treated with 0.1% DMSO.
claims.source: Under these conditions, we observed for both mutants a significant increase in Rb+ efflux in cells treated with Aekatperone in a dose-dependent manner compared with cells treated with 0.1% DMSO (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Cells treated overnight with the high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperone GBC followed by 30 min incubation in medium lacking GBC showed Rb+ efflux below that seen in cells treated overnight with the DMSO vehicle control.
claims.source: This is in stark contrast to cells treated overnight with the high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperone GBC followed by 30 min incubation in medium lacking GBC, where Rb+ efflux was below that seen in cells treated overnight with the DMSO vehicle control (note in DMSO-treated controls, there were still low levels of surface expression of the mutant channels to give rise to the low levels of efflux).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between Aekatperone and GBC effects.

claims.claim: Mutant-expressing cells treated overnight with Aekatperone followed by subsequent drug removal showed much greater diazoxide response, achieving up to 80% of the WT response.
claims.source: Significantly, mutant-expressing cells treated overnight with Aekatperone followed by subsequent drug removal showed much greater diazoxide response, achieving up to 80% of the WT response.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Including 10 μM Aekatperone had no significant effects on MgADP stimulation of SUR2A/Kir6.2 nor SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels.
claims.source: Inside-out patch-clamp recordings showed that including 10 μM Aekatperone had no significant effects on MgADP stimulation of SUR2A/Kir6.2 nor SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4A), indicating SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels are relatively insensitive to Aekatperone compared to SUR1/Kir6.2 channels.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The Aekatperone IC50 is 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels.
claims.source: The results yielded dose-response curves showing an Aekatperone IC50 of 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4B), which are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The Aekatperone IC50 for SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels.
claims.source: The results yielded dose-response curves showing an Aekatperone IC50 of 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4B), which are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 3D reconstruction of cryoEM particles of channels incubated with Aekatperone yielded a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
claims.source: 3D reconstruction of cryoEM particles of channels incubated with Aekatperone yielded a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the cryoEM structure determination.

claims.claim: A model built from the cryoEM map shows a closed Kir6.2 channel pore with a pore radius of ~0.75 Å at the helical bundle crossing residue F168 and an inward-facing SUR1 with NBDs separated.
claims.source: A model built from the map shows a closed Kir6.2 channel pore with a pore radius of ~0.75 Å at the helical bundle crossing residue F168 and an inward-facing SUR1 with NBDs separated, resembling other inhibitor-bound KATP channel structures reported to date (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: A clear nonprotein density consistent with the size of Aekatperone (MW: 399.52 g/mol) was observed in a TM pocket above NBD1 in the ABC core of SUR1.
claims.source: A clear nonprotein density consistent with the size of Aekatperone (MW: 399.52 g/mol) was observed in a TM pocket above NBD1 in the ABC core of SUR1 (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM density shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: Clear cryoEM density corresponding to the Kir6.2 distal N-terminal peptide domain (KNtp) was observed in between the two TM bundles of the SUR1-ABC core, with the very N-terminus of Kir6.2 contacting the bound Aekatperone.
claims.source: Moreover, as in the structures of KATP bound to GBC, RPG, or CBZ (Martin et al., 2019; Sung et al., 2022), we observed clear cryoEM density corresponding to the Kir6.2 distal N-terminal peptide domain (KNtp) in between the two TM bundles of the SUR1-ABC core, with the very N-terminus of Kir6.2 contacting the bound Aekatperone (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Stabilization of the KNtp-SUR1 interface promotes channel assembly, at the same time, it prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to an open conformation.
claims.source: Stabilization of the KNtp-SUR1 interface promotes channel assembly, at the same time, it prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to an open conformation (Driggers et al., 2024; Martin et al., 2019; Sung et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2018), which explains the dual chaperone and inhibitor activity of Aekatperone.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket.
claims.source: In this structural model, the cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket, and the imidazole group is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding conformation.

claims.claim: The imidazole group of Aekatperone is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
claims.source: In this structural model, the cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket, and the imidazole group is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding conformation.

claims.claim: The pyrazole moiety of Aekatperone has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245.
claims.source: The pyrazole moiety has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245, while the sulfonyl moiety is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

claims.claim: The sulfonyl moiety of Aekatperone is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
claims.source: The pyrazole moiety has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245, while the sulfonyl moiety is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

claims.claim: The benzene ring of Aekatperone forms a π–π stacking interaction with Y377 of SUR1.
claims.source: Moreover, the benzene ring of Aekatperone forms a π–π stacking interaction with Y377 of SUR1, and a series of hydrophobic interactions contributed by TM helices from both TMD1 (TM6, 7) and TMD2 (TM16, 17) help stabilize the benzene and cyclohexyl groups.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

results.result: AI-based virtual screening using AtomNet identified three promising KATP channel pharmacochaperone candidates from ~2.5 million compounds. The screening targeted the RPG binding site in the KATP channel structure (PDB ID 6PZ9), and after filtering and diversity clustering, 96 top-ranking compounds were tested experimentally, yielding three compounds (C24, C27, C45/Aekatperone) with consistent pharmacochaperone effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C33-C37, and C96-C99 describe a coherent virtual screening workflow with appropriate filtering steps (medicinal chemistry filters, similarity exclusion, diversity clustering). The identification of three active compounds from 96 tested candidates represents a reasonable hit rate (~3%) for structure-based virtual screening, and the methodology is well-documented with specific parameters provided.

results.result: Aekatperone exhibits pharmacochaperone effects on multiple KATP trafficking mutants. Western blot analysis showed that Aekatperone treatment (10-200 μM) increased the mature (complex-glycosylated) form of SUR1 trafficking mutants (F27S, A30T, A116P, V187D) in a dose-dependent manner, with effects plateauing at 100-200 μM. Immunofluorescence confirmed increased surface expression of mutant channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C40-C43 are well-supported by multiple complementary assays (western blot, immunofluorescence) across several trafficking mutants. The dose-response data (C41-C42) shows appropriate quantification with statistical analysis (n=3, p=0.0133). The use of multiple mutants strengthens the conclusion that Aekatperone has general pharmacochaperone activity for SUR1-TMD0 trafficking defects.

results.result: Aekatperone reversibly inhibits KATP channel activity with an IC50 of ~9 μM. Patch-clamp recordings showed that 10 μM Aekatperone occluded MgADP stimulation of KATP channels, but this effect was reversed upon compound washout. Rb+ efflux assays confirmed dose-dependent inhibition with IC50 = 9.23 ± 0.36 μM.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C44-C45, and C48 are supported by two independent assay methods (patch-clamp and Rb+ efflux) that yield consistent results. The reversibility demonstrated in C45 is a key finding distinguishing Aekatperone from high-affinity inhibitors like GBC. The IC50 determination includes appropriate error estimates and replication.

results.result: Trafficking mutant channels rescued by Aekatperone show functional recovery upon drug removal. After overnight Aekatperone treatment and washout, SUR1F27S and SUR1A30T mutants showed significant dose-dependent increases in Rb+ efflux compared to DMSO controls, contrasting with GBC-treated cells which showed reduced efflux. Rescued mutants responded to diazoxide at ~80% of wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C49-C51 demonstrate the key therapeutic advantage of Aekatperone over existing pharmacochaperones. The comparison with GBC (C50) provides critical context showing that high-affinity inhibitors prevent functional recovery. The diazoxide response data (C51) is particularly important for clinical relevance, though the exact experimental design could be clearer regarding timing of diazoxide addition.

results.result: Aekatperone's pharmacochaperone and reversible inhibitory effects are conserved in human KATP channels. The effects observed in hamster SUR1/rat Kir6.2 channels were replicated in human SUR1/Kir6.2 channels, which share 95% and 96% protein sequence identity, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing similar effects in human channels. The high sequence homology (C47) provides a reasonable basis for expecting conservation of drug effects. This is important for translational relevance, though more extensive characterization in human channels would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Aekatperone shows 4-5 fold selectivity for SUR1/Kir6.2 over SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels. Patch-clamp recordings showed that 10 μM Aekatperone had no significant effect on MgADP stimulation of SUR2-containing channels. Rb+ efflux assays yielded IC50 values of 41.22 ± 2.22 μM (SUR2A) and 41.85 ± 2.08 μM (SUR2B), compared to 9.2 μM for SUR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C75 are well-supported by both electrophysiology and Rb+ efflux data showing consistent ~4-5 fold selectivity. The selectivity is modest but potentially sufficient to reduce off-target effects on cardiac and smooth muscle KATP channels. Statistical analysis and replication appear adequate, though the number of replicates is not explicitly stated for all experiments.

results.result: CryoEM structure of Aekatperone-bound KATP channel was determined at 4.1 Å resolution. The structure shows a closed Kir6.2 pore (radius ~0.75 Å at F168), NBD-separated SUR1 conformation, and clear density for Aekatperone in the TMD pocket above NBD1. The Kir6.2 N-terminal peptide (KNtp) is resolved with its N-terminus contacting bound Aekatperone.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 and C10 describe a well-characterized cryoEM structure with appropriate resolution for the conclusions drawn. The 4.1 Å resolution is sufficient to identify ligand density and overall protein conformations. The structure determination workflow (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) shows appropriate particle numbers and classification steps. Comparison with apo structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) validates ligand assignment.

results.result: Aekatperone binds in the SUR1 TMD pocket with distinct features compared to high-affinity inhibitors. The cyclohexyl moiety aligns with S1238, the pyrazole coordinates with T1242/N1245, the sulfonyl group interacts with R1246/R1300, and the benzene ring forms π-π stacking with Y377. Unlike GBC and RPG, Aekatperone does not interact with R306. This binding stabilizes the KNtp-SUR1 interface, promoting assembly while preventing channel opening.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 describe detailed molecular interactions supported by the cryoEM structure. However, C59 relies heavily on citations to prior work for the mechanistic interpretation. The lack of R306 interaction (C65) is an important distinguishing feature. The resolution (4.1 Å) is marginal for confidently assigning all specific interactions, particularly for the imidazole group which shows weaker density (acknowledged in the text).

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal conformational flexibility of Aekatperone in the binding pocket. During 2.5 μs of simulation (5 × 500 ns runs), Aekatperone remained in the pocket but exhibited flexibility, particularly in the imidazole ring (group e) which displayed considerable conformational freedom.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by MD simulation data with appropriate total simulation time (2.5 μs across 5 replicates). The analysis of conformational freedom by molecular fragments is appropriate. The flexibility of the imidazole group (C67) is consistent with the weaker cryoEM density for this region. System equilibration appears adequate based on Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Mutagenesis validates the Aekatperone binding model. Mutations Y377A, R1246A, and R1300A significantly reduced Aekatperone inhibition, with Y377A and R1300A being particularly detrimental. R306A had little effect, consistent with lack of R306 involvement. The S1238Y/T1242S double mutation (mimicking SUR2) reduced inhibition, and Kir6.2 N-terminal deletions (ΔN5, ΔN10) attenuated inhibition at all concentrations tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide strong functional validation of the structural model through systematic mutagenesis. The results are internally consistent with the binding model and the selectivity data. Statistical analysis appears appropriate with multiple replicates. The KNtp deletion experiments (C72) support involvement of the N-terminus, though they cannot distinguish between direct binding interactions and allosteric effects on channel gating.

results.result: Aekatperone represents a promising lead compound for CHI treatment and validates AI-aided drug discovery for rare diseases. The compound fits the profile of a reversible inhibitor pharmacochaperone with selectivity for pancreatic KATP channels, and rescued mutant channels respond to diazoxide at ~80% of wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 and C78 represent conclusions and future directions rather than fully demonstrated results. While the data support Aekatperone's potential (C73-C74), clinical application requires extensive additional validation not yet performed (acknowledged in C94-C95). The claim about AI-aided drug discovery (C78) is supported by the successful identification of active compounds, but the comparison to traditional methods is not rigorously evaluated.

results.result: Background on KATP channels, CHI, and pharmacochaperones. KATP channels (SUR1/Kir6.2) regulate insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells. Loss-of-function mutations cause CHI, with trafficking mutations being unresponsive to diazoxide. Current KATP inhibitors act as pharmacochaperones but have high affinity that limits functional recovery. Structural studies revealed a common binding pocket in SUR1 where inhibitors stabilize the SUR1-Kir6.2 interface.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C32 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the mechanistic understanding is consistent with current knowledge in the field.

results.result: Aekatperone is classified as a 'site A' ligand based on structural comparison with other KATP inhibitors. This classification is supported by Aekatperone occupying the site A region and the S1238Y mutation compromising inhibition. Site A ligands show variable potency, with tolbutamide and Aekatperone being reversible (IC50 ~23 μM and 9 μM), while mitiglinide is nearly irreversible (IC50 in low nM range).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 provide useful context by relating Aekatperone to the established site A/B binding model. The classification is supported by structural and mutagenesis data (C80). The comparison with other site A ligands (C81-C82) appropriately cites prior work and highlights that site occupancy alone does not determine affinity or reversibility.

results.result: Discussion of CHI therapeutic landscape and limitations of existing pharmacochaperones. Nearly half of CHI-KATP mutations prevent surface expression. KATP trafficking mutations concentrate in SUR1-TMD0 and are rescued by various inhibitors (tolbutamide, GBC, RPG, CBZ). However, GBC and RPG have high affinity preventing functional recovery, CBZ has multiple off-targets, and tolbutamide was withdrawn due to cardiovascular concerns.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C92 summarize the therapeutic context and limitations of existing drugs, appropriately citing prior literature. These claims justify the need for new pharmacochaperones like Aekatperone but represent discussion/context rather than novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Study limitations and future directions. The focused screening approach may miss potential scaffolds from larger libraries. Before clinical application, Aekatperone requires evaluation for off-target effects, testing in relevant cell and animal models, and assessment of potential cardiovascular/neurological effects. A dosing regimen combining Aekatperone with diazoxide could enhance therapeutic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 and C93-C95 appropriately acknowledge study limitations and propose future directions. These are reasonable assessments of what additional work is needed. C93 is speculative but logically follows from the data. C94-C95 correctly identify that extensive additional validation is required before clinical translation.

results.result: Cell line authentication and quality control. COSm6 cells were authenticated by RT-PCR/sequencing of α-tubulin (confirming Green monkey origin), and INS-1 cells by RT-PCR/sequencing of SUR1 and Kir6.2 (confirming rat origin). Both cell lines were tested for mycoplasma contamination every ~6 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 describe appropriate cell line authentication and quality control procedures. These are important methodological details that support reproducibility and data integrity. The authentication methods are standard and appropriate for the cell lines used.

results.result: The authors used AI-based virtual screening (AtomNet) to screen ~2.5 million compounds against the repaglinide binding site in KATP channels, identifying 96 top candidates. After functional validation, three compounds (C24, C27, C45) showed pharmacochaperone effects, with C45 (Aekatperone) demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition and reversibility.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the AI screening approach and experimental validation. Reviewer 1 states 'The experimental work confirming that Aekatperone acts to traffic mutant KATP channels to the surface...is comprehensive and clear, with very convincing cell biological and patch-clamp data.' Reviewer 2 notes the 'computational screening of a large virtual compound library, followed by functional screening' as a main strength. The editor confirms 'screening by artificial intelligence can identify relevant novel compounds.'

results.result: Aekatperone exhibits pharmacochaperone effects on multiple KATP trafficking mutants (SUR1F27S, SUR1A30T, SUR1A116P, SUR1V187D), rescuing surface expression in a dose-dependent manner. At 200 μM, rescue of SUR1A30T reached 64% of WT levels. These effects were observed in both hamster/rat and human KATP channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'The experimental work confirming that Aekatperone acts to traffic mutant KATP channels to the surface...is comprehensive and clear, with very convincing cell biological and patch-clamp data.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the drug clearly rescues cell surface expression' as a main finding. No concerns were raised about the pharmacochaperone data.

results.result: Aekatperone reversibly inhibits KATP channels with an IC50 of ~9 μM. The compound occludes MgADP stimulation, but channel function recovers upon washout, demonstrating reversibility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support the reversibility findings. Reviewer 1 describes Aekatperone as 'a low affinity, reversible inhibitor' with 'very convincing...patch-clamp data.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes that the drug 'can be readily washed off in patch clamp, and cell based efflux assays' as a key strength. The reversibility is central to the therapeutic rationale and is not questioned.

results.result: Mutant channels rescued by Aekatperone show functional recovery upon drug washout. After overnight Aekatperone treatment and washout, rescued mutant channels respond to diazoxide, achieving up to 80% of WT response, contrasting with high-affinity inhibitor GBC which prevents functional recovery.
results.evaluation: This is a critical finding strongly endorsed by reviewers. Reviewer 2 states 'the drug clearly rescues cell surface expression, but can be manipulated experimentally to permit function of rescued channels' and notes this as important for therapeutic application. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the contrast with high-affinity inhibitors. The functional recovery after washout is central to the paper's therapeutic promise.

results.result: CryoEM structure of KATP bound to Aekatperone at 4.1 Å resolution reveals distinct binding features compared to high-affinity inhibitors. Aekatperone binds in the SUR1 ABC core pocket, stabilizing the KNtp-SUR1 interface. Unlike GBC and RPG, Aekatperone does not interact with R306, occupying a more limited binding space.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the structural findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the cryoEM structural analysis, for which the group are leading experts' is 'comprehensive and clear.' Reviewer 2 lists 'Determination of the binding site and dynamics of this candidate drug by cryo-EM' as a main finding with 'well-conceived and executed' experiments. The structural differences from known inhibitors are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations over 2.5 μs show Aekatperone remains in the binding pocket but exhibits flexibility, particularly in the imidazole ring which displays considerable conformational freedom.
results.evaluation: The MD simulation data is presented as supporting evidence for the structural model and is not questioned by reviewers. Reviewer 2 mentions 'functional validation of several residues involved in drug sensitivity using mutagenesis' which complements the MD findings. The simulations are treated as part of the comprehensive structural characterization.

results.result: Mutagenesis studies validate the Aekatperone binding model. Y377A and R1300A mutations severely impair inhibition, while R306A has minimal effect. S1238Y/T1242S and Kir6.2 N-terminal deletions (ΔN5, ΔN10) significantly reduce Aekatperone sensitivity, confirming the importance of these residues and the KNtp interaction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse the mutagenesis validation. Reviewer 2 states 'functional validation of several residues involved in drug sensitivity using mutagenesis and patch clamp' is well-executed. Reviewer 1 notes the group's expertise in functional studies. The mutagenesis data directly supports the structural model and is accepted without criticism.

results.result: Aekatperone shows ~4-5 fold selectivity for SUR1/Kir6.2 (IC50 ~9 μM) over SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (IC50 ~41 μM), with minimal effects on cardiac and smooth muscle KATP isoforms at concentrations effective for pancreatic channels.
results.evaluation: The selectivity data is accepted by reviewers as an important feature. Reviewer 2 notes the experiments are 'well-conceived and executed' and the selectivity is relevant to therapeutic application. While reviewers acknowledge that cardiovascular effects need evaluation (see C94), the functional selectivity data itself is not questioned.

results.result: The authors conclude that Aekatperone is a promising lead compound for CHI treatment due to its reversible inhibition profile and selectivity, and that AI-aided virtual screening is an emerging strategy for drug discovery in rare diseases. They propose a dosing regimen combining Aekatperone with diazoxide.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express mixed views on therapeutic promise. Reviewer 1 questions 'whether the new compound will offer advantages over earlier low-affinity sulfonylurea inhibitor chaperones' like tolbutamide and raises concerns about 'potential adverse cardiovascular effects.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'a challenging relationship between efficacy of trafficking rescue and channel inhibition' that 'will need to be overcome.' However, both reviewers recognize the conceptual advance and potential, with the editor noting 'the broader significance...relates to the possibility that KATP channel mutations...may be effectively rescued.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including that their focused library approach may miss potential scaffolds, that Aekatperone requires rigorous evaluation for cardiovascular and neurological effects, and that translation to clinical applications requires extensive additional studies in relevant models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly raise these concerns and the authors' acknowledgment is appropriate. Reviewer 1 states 'it is unclear why Aekatperone should not have the same concerns' as tolbutamide regarding cardiovascular effects. Reviewer 2 notes 'it is straightforward to wash off the chaperone, but this would not be the case in an organism' and emphasizes the need to investigate 'underlying mechanisms' and 'ways to manipulate them.' The limitations are recognized by all parties.
